title: PV Basket Cells
intro: Parvalbumin-expressing basket cells are the cortex's fast inhibitory neurons. Their axons form baskets of synapses around the somata of pyramidal cells, they fire narrow spikes at hundreds of hertz without slowing down, and they are recruited within a millisecond or two of any excitation. They set the timing of cortical activity, keep excitation in balance and generate gamma oscillations.

items: Morphology: multipolar, aspiny or sparsely spiny dendrites; an axon that branches densely within a few hundred micrometres and makes many synapses on the somata and proximal dendrites of each target. Blue Brain distinguishes large, nest and small basket cells by axon spread.

Firing: fast spiking. Action potentials of about 0.2 to 0.4 ms half-width, followed by a deep, fast after-hyperpolarisation; sustained rates above 200 Hz with little adaptation. The key channels are Kv3.1/Kv3.2 potassium channels, which open only at depolarised voltages and close quickly (Rudy & McBain 2001).
Passive properties: low input resistance and short membrane time constant (about 5 to 10 ms), so they integrate over a narrow time window and act as coincidence detectors.

Inputs: strong, fast, depressing excitation from local pyramidal and layer 4 cells and from the thalamus, through AMPA receptors with GluA4-rich, fast-kinetics subunits; inhibition from other PV cells and SST cells; electrical synapses (gap junctions) with other PV cells (Galarreta & Hestrin 1999; Gibson, Beierlein & Connors 1999).

Outputs: fast GABA-A synapses (decay about 2 to 5 ms) on almost every pyramidal cell nearby, with connection probabilities often above 0.5 within 100 µm (Packer & Yuste 2011). This dense, non-selective 'blanket of inhibition' is a defining feature.
Myelinated axons, high metabolic demand and perineuronal nets around the soma are further hallmarks; PV cell maturation closes critical periods of plasticity in visual cortex (Hensch 2005).

Feedforward inhibition: input excites PV cells and pyramidal cells together; PV inhibition arrives about 1 to 2 ms later and cuts off further integration, so pyramidal cells respond only to synchronous input (Pouille & Scanziani 2001).

Feedback inhibition and E/I balance: PV inhibition tracks excitation within milliseconds, so each pyramidal cell sees large excitatory and inhibitory conductances that nearly cancel, the balanced state.

Gamma oscillations: mutually inhibiting, gap-junction coupled PV cells, or PV cells interacting with pyramidal cells (the PING mechanism), generate 30 to 80 Hz rhythms. Optogenetic drive of PV cells creates gamma in vivo (Cardin et al. 2009; Sohal et al. 2009).
Gain and competition: by inhibiting broadly, PV cells implement divisive or subtractive gain control (Atallah et al. 2012; Wilson et al. 2012 debated which) and winner-take-all competition.

Wang and Buzsaki (1996): the classic single-compartment conductance model of a hippocampal fast-spiking basket cell (sodium, delayed-rectifier potassium and leak, with fast kinetics). Networks of these cells, coupled by GABA-A synapses, synchronise at gamma frequencies; it remains the default 'interneuron gamma' (ING) model.
Erisir et al. (1999): an HH-type model showing that a Kv3-like potassium current is what makes fast spiking possible.

Izhikevich (2003) fast-spiking preset: a = 0.1, b = 0.2, c = −65, d = 2. Izhikevich (2007) also gives a version with a nonlinear u-nullcline that reproduces the abrupt onset of firing (type 2 excitability) of real FS cells.
Pospischil et al. (2008) give a minimal HH model of cortical fast-spiking cells fitted to recordings; Blue Brain's LBC, NBC and SBC m-types with cNAC and bAC e-types are the detailed versions.
Network models: PING models (Borgers & Kopell 2003; Brunel & Wang 2003), and the inhibitory population in Brunel (2000) and Potjans-Diesmann (2014), are effectively PV-like cells with fast synapses.

blocks.text: Try it: fast spiking versus regular spiking

Switch between the fast-spiking and regular-spiking presets of the Izhikevich model. The fast-spiking cell fires faster at the same current and its interspike intervals stay constant, because its recovery variable u decays quickly (a = 0.1) and each spike adds little to it (d = 2).
What this means for your SNN

items: Your inhibitory population should be fast: membrane time constant around 5 to 10 ms, GABA-A synapses decaying in a few ms, little or no adaptation, short synaptic delays.

Connect it densely and non-selectively to nearby excitatory cells (p ≈ 0.3 to 0.6), and give it strong input from those same cells; this is what enforces sparse, balanced activity and k-WTA competition.
Feed thalamic or input-layer spikes to PV cells as well as to excitatory cells to get feedforward inhibition and precise timing.
If you want gamma rhythms, add PV-to-PV inhibition (and optionally gap junctions).
